note.question: How should enrollment timing in early-stage patient-centered clinical trials be designed?
note.overview: Early-stage patient-centered clinical trials aim to establish the toxicity profile of investigational drugs and determine safe dose ranges for future trials using cohort-specific consent. Patients considering participation face intricate benefit-risk tradeoffs, particularly regarding the timing of their enrollment: Early enrollment corresponds to low doses with potentially low efficacy and toxicity with high uncertainty around them, whereas late enrollment corresponds to high doses with potentially high efficacy and toxicity with reduced uncertainty, but also an increased risk of disease progression and trial termination. We also establish sufficient conditions for the existence of a control-limit enrollment time policy based on the patient’s health status and beliefs.

source.quote: Problem definition: Early-stage patient-centered clinical trials aim to establish the toxicity profile of investigational drugs and determine safe dose ranges for future trials using cohort-specific consent.

Model Overview In the model, a patient diagnosed with a condition, for example, lung cancer, makes periodic visits to a medi­ cal facility for follow-up care and serves as the decision maker (DM) to differentiate from other patients.
Nonetheless, our model can be extended so that the realization of efficacy and toxicity may be dependent to the health status by expanding the state space and considering a larger prior covari­ ance.
Case Study This section demonstrates the implications of applying the proposed enrollment policy within a Phase I CT for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Note that in 3+3 there are potentially two cohorts of patients, as in the simulation, but in our model we only allow decision making for a patient before the initiation of a dose.
The patient periodically learns about the benefits and risks of doses and enrolls in the trial at the optimal time to maximize the expected benefits.
